tracks.name: Tailwind CSS
tracks.description: Build interfaces with utility classes instead of custom CSS.

lessons.title: 1. Utility Classes and Setup
lessons.summary: Load Tailwind and style your first element with utility classes.

activities.title: Chaining utility classes
activities.instruction: Tailwind styles an element by combining small utility classes in its `class` attribute. `p-4` adds padding, `bg-slate-900` sets a dark background, `text-white` makes the text readable, and `rounded-lg` softens the corners.

activities.title: Which class rounds the corners?
activities.question: Which utility class gives an element large rounded corners?
activities.explanation: The `rounded-*` utilities control corner radius. `text-lg` changes font size and `border-lg` is not a Tailwind class.

teaching.text: Tailwind CSS is a **utility-first** framework. Instead of writing custom CSS rules, you combine small single-purpose classes directly on your HTML elements.
The quickest way to try Tailwind is the CDN build. Add this script inside `<head>`:
<script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>
Now any Tailwind class you add is styled. Each class does one job, and you compose them to build the result:
Hello Tailwind
That single `class` attribute replaces a block of custom CSS. `p-4` is padding, `bg-slate-900` is a near-black background, `text-white` is white text, and `rounded-lg` is a large corner radius.
Utility classes only work when Tailwind is loaded. On a real project you would install Tailwind with a build step, but the CDN is perfect for learning and quick prototypes.

lessons.title: 2. Spacing and Flexbox
lessons.summary: Use the spacing scale and flex utilities to arrange a toolbar.

activities.title: A flex toolbar
activities.instruction: `flex` turns a container into a row. `items-center` aligns children vertically, `justify-between` pushes them to opposite ends, and `gap-4` adds space between them without margins.
activities.example: Team

activities.title: What does gap-4 do?
activities.question: In a flex container, what does `gap-4` add?
activities.explanation: `gap-*` controls the space between flex or grid children. It is usually cleaner than adding margins to every child.

teaching.text: Tailwind's spacing scale gives every value a number. `p-4` is padding, `px-4` is horizontal padding, `py-2` is vertical padding, and `m-2` is margin. Bigger numbers mean more space.
Flexbox utilities handle alignment. `flex` creates a row, `items-center` aligns items on the cross axis, `justify-between` spreads them apart, and `gap-4` spaces them evenly:
Team
Use `gap-*` instead of margins when spacing a row or grid. There is no leftover margin on the first or last child.

lessons.title: 3. Typography, Borders, and Shadows
lessons.summary: Style text, borders, and depth with utility classes.

activities.title: A profile card
activities.instruction: Typography utilities set size and weight, while border and shadow utilities add structure and depth. `text-2xl` is a large heading, `font-bold` adds weight, `border` draws a border, and `shadow-lg` lifts the card off the page.
activities.example:
Ada Lovelace

Mathematician

activities.title: Which class makes text larger?
activities.question: Which utility increases the font size of a heading?
activities.explanation: `text-*` controls font size (and can also set color). `font-bold` changes weight and `border-2` changes border width.

teaching.text: Tailwind includes a full color palette and a type scale. Use `text-slate-900` for strong text, `text-slate-500` for secondary text, and `text-2xl` or `text-sm` to control size.

Ada Lovelace

Mathematician
Borders and shadows separate content from the page. `border` adds a 1px border, `border-slate-200` colors it, `rounded-xl` rounds the corners, and `shadow-lg` adds depth:

Ada Lovelace

Mathematician

Available
`max-w-sm` caps the card width. Pair it with `p-6` and the card stays comfortable on both mobile and desktop.

lessons.title: 4. Hover and Focus States
lessons.summary: Add clear feedback to buttons and links with state variants.

activities.title: A button with feedback
activities.instruction: State variants apply a utility only in a specific situation. `hover:bg-indigo-700` darkens the button when the pointer is over it, while `focus:ring-2` draws a ring when the button has keyboard focus.
activities.example:
<button class="px-5 py-3 bg-indigo-600 text-white font-semibold rounded-lg hover:bg-indigo-700 focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-300 transition">
  Save changes
</button>

activities.title: Which prefix means hover?
activities.question: Which class applies only while the pointer is over the element?
activities.explanation: The `hover:` prefix applies the utility on hover. `active:` is for the pressed state and `focus:` is for keyboard or click focus.

teaching.text: Interactive elements should tell the user when they are hovered or focused. Tailwind's state variants let you add a whole utility only for that state:

<button class="bg-indigo-600 hover:bg-indigo-700">
  Save changes
</button>

Keyboard users need a visible focus ring too. `focus:ring-2` adds a ring and `focus:ring-indigo-300` sets its color. `focus:outline-none` removes the browser default so the Tailwind ring is the only indicator:

<button class="focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-300">
  Save changes
</button>
Add `transition` so color and ring changes animate smoothly instead of snapping:

<button class="transition hover:bg-indigo-700 focus:ring-2">
  Save changes
</button>
Never remove focus styles without replacing them. `focus:ring-*` is the accessible replacement for `outline: none`.

lessons.title: 5. Responsive Layouts
lessons.summary: Build mobile-first layouts that change at Tailwind breakpoints.

activities.title: A responsive card grid
activities.instruction: Responsive prefixes apply a utility from a breakpoint upward. `grid-cols-1` is the mobile default, `sm:grid-cols-2` switches to two columns on small screens, and `lg:grid-cols-3` switches to three on large screens.
activities.example:
Card One
Card Two
Card Three

activities.title: When does md: apply?
activities.question: What does `md:grid-cols-2` mean?
choices: Use two columns only on screens smaller than the md breakpoint
Use two columns from the md breakpoint upward
Use two columns on every screen size
activities.answer: Use two columns from the md breakpoint upward
activities.explanation: Tailwind is mobile-first. An unprefixed utility is the base style, and a prefixed utility like `md:` applies from that breakpoint upward.

teaching.text: Tailwind layouts are **mobile-first**. Write the base layout with unprefixed classes, then add larger-screen refinements with `sm:`, `md:`, `lg:`, and `xl:`.
Default breakpoints:
Prefixes work with any utility, not just grid columns. This heading is large on mobile and larger from `md` upward:
Responsive Cards
Because prefixes stack upward, you usually only need one class per breakpoint. `grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` already covers every larger screen.
